passage.title: Grain of the Cedar Rib
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Sawdust floated in the golden light of the barn as Jonah and his older brother, Marcus, knelt beside their grandfather's wooden canoe. For ten summers, the sixteen-foot craft had carried them across Lake Rabun. Now a cracked rib near the bow needed repair before Saturday's trip. Jonah ran his hand over the smooth cedar planks. He admired how every brass tack lined up in a neat row. He wanted their repair to match the quiet pride their grandfather had built into the hull.

Marcus, however, kept glancing at his watch and tapping a can of quick-setting paste. From Marcus's viewpoint, spending three nights steaming and bending a fresh strip of white cedar was a waste of time when no one would look under the rim. He argued that a thick scoop of gray paste would harden in twenty minutes and get them onto the lake by noon. Jonah shook his head. Stiff paste would crack the first time the flexible wooden hull bent against a wave.

To settle the dispute, Jonah lifted the broken section to show why the old rib had failed after a rocky landing last autumn. The split cedar rib, weakened by winter moisture trapped beneath a patched coat of paint, was carefully pried from the hull by Jonah with a flat chisel. Under the old patch, someone had once smeared hard putty instead of putting in new wood. Instead of bonding with the cedar, the stiff lump had pulled away from the planks and trapped lake water against the grain.

Seeing the dark, softened wood under the old shortcut made Marcus set his can of paste back on the shelf. He admitted that a fast patch today would only rot two more planks by next spring. Together, the brothers filled the iron steamer kettle and slid a fresh strip of white cedar into the hot mist. When the wood grew pliable, Marcus helped Jonah clamp the curve smoothly against the hull.

By Friday night, a coat of clear marine varnish gleamed over the new rib. At dawn, they carried the canoe down to the dock. The hull felt light, tight, and balanced on their shoulders. Marcus grinned and thanked his younger brother for being stubborn enough to protect their grandfather's boat. Out on the glassy water, the cedar planks flexed gently with every stroke of their paddles.

monsterSentence.verbatimSentence: The split cedar rib, weakened by winter moisture trapped beneath a patched coat of paint, was carefully pried from the hull by Jonah with a flat chisel.
distractorChunks: weakened by winter moisture trapped beneath a patched coat of paint
monsterSentence.activeRewrite: Jonah carefully pried the split cedar rib from the hull with a flat chisel.

tier2Words.definition: a person's way of thinking about or looking at a situation
tier2Words.rootHint: Compound word combining view ('to see') + point ('position')
tier2Words.contextClue: Marcus saw the repair differently than Jonah and thought steaming new wood was a waste of time.

tier2Words.definition: able to bend easily without breaking or cracking
tier2Words.contextClue: Unlike stiff paste that would crack, the wood hull bent gently when hitting a wave.

tier2Words.definition: easy to bend and shape without snapping
tier2Words.rootHint: Latin root plicare ('to fold or bend')
tier2Words.contextClue: After sitting in the hot mist of the kettle, the cedar strip bent smoothly against the curve of the hull.

tier2Words.definition: shone brightly with a smooth, clean light
tier2Words.rootHint: Old English glaem ('bright beam or glow')
tier2Words.contextClue: A fresh coat of clear marine varnish shone brightly over the newly repaired cedar rib.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"The split cedar rib, weakened by winter moisture trapped beneath a patched coat of paint, was carefully pried from the hull by Jonah with a flat chisel."

Based on the sentence structure, what damaged the cedar rib, and who removed it from the canoe?

options.text: Jonah weakened the cedar rib with a flat chisel, and winter moisture pried it from the hull.
options.childFeedback: This swaps the two causes! Trapped winter moisture is what weakened the split cedar rib, and Jonah is the person who pried it out with a chisel.

options.text: A flat chisel trapped the winter moisture until the patched coat of paint pried itself loose.
options.childFeedback: A metal chisel did not trap winter moisture, and a coat of paint cannot pry itself loose from a canoe!

options.text: Winter moisture trapped under paint weakened the rib, and Jonah pried it out using a flat chisel.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, 'weakened by winter moisture' and 'was carefully pried from the hull by Jonah with a flat chisel' show that trapped winter moisture weakened the cedar rib and Jonah pried it out.

options.text: Marcus broke the cedar rib by dropping the iron kettle inside the wooden hull.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 says the old rib failed after a rocky landing last autumn and rotted from trapped moisture—not because Marcus dropped the steamer kettle.

questions.provingSentenceText: The split cedar rib, weakened by winter moisture trapped beneath a patched coat of paint, was carefully pried from the hull by Jonah with a flat chisel.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, 'weakened by winter moisture' and 'was carefully pried from the hull by Jonah with a flat chisel' show that trapped winter moisture weakened the cedar rib and Jonah pried it out.
questions.parentExplanation: This passive sentence contains two 'by' phrases: 'weakened by winter moisture' explains what damaged the wood, and 'was carefully pried from the hull by Jonah' identifies who removed it.
questions.retryHint: Check the two 'by' phrases in Paragraph 3: 'weakened by...' and 'was carefully pried from the hull by...'

questions.prompt:
Read these sentences from Paragraph 4:

"Together, the brothers filled the iron steamer kettle and slid a fresh strip of white cedar into the hot mist. When the wood grew pliable, Marcus helped Jonah clamp the curve smoothly against the hull."

What does the word pliable mean as it is used in Paragraph 4?

options.text: Softened and easy to bend into a smooth curve
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, 'pliable' means softened and easy to bend into a smooth curve, because steaming the white cedar strip in hot mist made it flexible enough to clamp smoothly against the curved hull.

options.text: Brittle and likely to snap into sharp splinters
options.childFeedback: Brittle and likely to snap is the opposite of 'pliable'—the brothers steamed the cedar specifically so it would bend smoothly without snapping.

options.text: Covered in thick gray paste from a metal can
options.childFeedback: Marcus already set his can of gray paste back on the shelf at the start of Paragraph 4 before they steamed the fresh white cedar strip.

options.text: Heavy enough to sink the canoe to the lake bottom
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 5 says the repaired canoe hull felt light, tight, and balanced on their shoulders and floated out on the glassy water.

questions.provingSentenceText: When the wood grew pliable, Marcus helped Jonah clamp the curve smoothly against the hull.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, 'pliable' means softened and easy to bend into a smooth curve, because steaming the white cedar strip in hot mist made it flexible enough to clamp smoothly against the curved hull.
questions.parentExplanation: After being steamed in hot mist, the cedar strip could be clamped smoothly into a curve against the hull, showing that 'pliable' means bendable and supple.
questions.retryHint: Think about what hot steam does to a strip of wood so the brothers can 'clamp the curve smoothly against the hull' in Paragraph 4.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 3, what finally convinces Marcus to give up his plan of using quick paste?

options.text: He discovers that the hardware store is completely sold out of gray paste.
options.childFeedback: Marcus already has a can of quick-setting gray paste in his hand in Paragraph 2, and he puts it back on the shelf in Paragraph 4.

options.text: He worries that brass tacks will rust if they ever touch clear marine varnish.
options.childFeedback: Brass tacks and clear marine varnish work fine together on the canoe; what changes Marcus's mind is seeing the dark, softened wood under the old putty patch.

options.text: He realizes that steaming white cedar takes only five minutes instead of three nights.
options.childFeedback: Steaming, clamping, and varnishing the new cedar rib still takes until Friday night; Marcus simply realizes the slow way is worth the time.

options.text: He sees that an older putty shortcut had pulled away from the planks and trapped water against the wood.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraphs 3 and 4, when Jonah pries up the broken rib, Marcus sees that an old hard-putty shortcut had pulled away from the planks, trapped lake water, and rotted the wood underneath.

questions.provingSentenceText: Instead of bonding with the cedar, the stiff lump had pulled away from the planks and trapped lake water against the grain.
questions.childTip: In Paragraphs 3 and 4, when Jonah pries up the broken rib, Marcus sees that an old hard-putty shortcut had pulled away from the planks, trapped lake water, and rotted the wood underneath.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 3, Jonah pries off the broken rib and reveals that an old putty patch had pulled away from the cedar and trapped water, which convinces Marcus in Paragraph 4 to put his can away.
questions.retryHint: Look at the end of Paragraph 3 and the first sentence of Paragraph 4 to see what Jonah uncovered under the old patch.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator's point of view in Paragraph 2 help the reader understand the conflict between the brothers?

options.text: By showing that neither brother cares about their granddad's canoe anymore
options.childFeedback: Both brothers want to take the canoe out on Lake Rabun on Saturday, and Jonah cares deeply about matching their grandfather's careful craftsmanship.

options.text: By contrasting Marcus's desire for a quick fix with Jonah's knowledge of how a wood hull moves on the water
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the third-person narrator shows both brothers' thoughts—contrasting Marcus's impatience for a twenty-minute paste fix with Jonah's understanding that stiff paste would crack when the flexible wood hull bends.

options.text: By telling the entire story in the first person through the granddad's journal entries
options.childFeedback: The story is told in the third person ('Jonah,' 'Marcus,' 'he'), not through first-person journal entries written by their grandfather.

options.text: By explaining that Jonah wants to sell the canoe as soon as the paint dries
options.childFeedback: Neither brother wants to sell the canoe; they are repairing it for Saturday's trip on Lake Rabun and want to protect their grandfather's boat.

questions.provingSentenceText: From Marcus's viewpoint, spending three nights steaming and bending a fresh strip of white cedar was a waste of time when no one would look under the rim.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the third-person narrator shows both brothers' thoughts—contrasting Marcus's impatience for a twenty-minute paste fix with Jonah's understanding that stiff paste would crack when the flexible wood hull bends.
questions.parentExplanation: The third-person narrator reveals both brothers' perspectives in Paragraph 2 (ELAGSE5RL6): Marcus focuses on saving time with a hidden patch, while Jonah focuses on structural integrity.
questions.retryHint: Compare 'From Marcus's viewpoint...' in the first half of Paragraph 2 with Jonah's response at the end of Paragraph 2.

questions.prompt: Part A: Which statement best expresses a central theme of the story?

options.text: Wooden canoes cannot float on Lake Rabun unless they are painted every Saturday.
options.childFeedback: The canoe had carried them for ten summers and only needed a new cedar rib and varnish after a rocky landing—not paint every single Saturday.

options.text: Older brothers should always let younger brothers do all the heavy work in a barn.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, both brothers work together to fill the steamer kettle and clamp the new cedar strip into place.

options.text: Doing a job the right way takes patience, whereas careless shortcuts often create worse damage later.
options.childFeedback: The story teaches that taking the time to do a repair the right way (steaming and bending real cedar) protects what matters, whereas quick shortcuts (like hard putty) cause worse damage over time.

options.text: Quick-setting paste is stronger and more flexible than steamed white cedar.
options.childFeedback: Paragraphs 2 and 3 prove the exact opposite: stiff paste pulls away from flexible wood planks and traps water that rots the hull.

questions.provingSentenceText: He admitted that a fast patch today would only rot two more planks by next spring.
questions.childTip: The story teaches that taking the time to do a repair the right way (steaming and bending real cedar) protects what matters, whereas quick shortcuts (like hard putty) cause worse damage over time.
questions.parentExplanation: The central theme contrasts patient craftsmanship with hasty shortcuts, highlighted when Marcus recognizes that a quick patch today would cause worse rot by next spring.
questions.retryHint: Look at what Marcus admits in Paragraph 4 about a 'fast patch today' versus why he thanks Jonah in Paragraph 5.

questions.prompt: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "He admitted that a fast patch today would only rot two more planks by next spring."
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 4 directly proves Question 5 by showing Marcus's realization that taking a quick shortcut today would only cause worse damage ('rot two more planks') by next spring.

options.text: "For ten summers, the sixteen-foot craft had carried them across Lake Rabun."
options.childFeedback: This detail from Paragraph 1 only tells how many summers the family had used the canoe on Lake Rabun.

options.text: "By Friday night, a coat of clear marine varnish gleamed over the new rib."
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 5 only describes the shiny varnish on Friday night after the repair was finished.

options.text: "Out on the glassy water, the cedar planks flexed gently with every stroke of their paddles."
options.childFeedback: This closing line from Paragraph 5 describes the canoe gliding on the lake, without stating the lesson about why shortcuts fail.

questions.provingSentenceText: He admitted that a fast patch today would only rot two more planks by next spring.
questions.childTip: This sentence from Paragraph 4 directly proves Question 5 by showing Marcus's realization that taking a quick shortcut today would only cause worse damage ('rot two more planks') by next spring.
questions.parentExplanation: Option B directly supports the theme in Part A by showing how a hasty shortcut leads to greater damage over time.
